units.title: Values, names & first steps
units.summary: Store values, work with numbers, and make your first output.
lesson: A variable name refers to a value. In Python, = assigns a value and == compares two values. Strings use quotes; integers such as 3 do not. print() displays a value.

input() returns a string, even when the learner types digits. Use int() to convert a string containing an integer before doing arithmetic. An invalid integer string raises ValueError; our exercises use valid numeric strings.
units.takeaway: Convert numeric text before arithmetic; assignment and comparison are different operations.

units.title: Transform data with comprehensions
units.summary: Filter a sequence and build a result without mutating your input.
lesson: A list comprehension creates a new list from an iterable: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. The if clause filters input items; the expression transforms the items that remain. The original list is not modified by the comprehension.
Functions return results with return. A function that only prints its result returns None implicitly. Keep transformation and display separate so callers can reuse the data.
units.takeaway: The filter chooses items; the leading expression transforms them. Return data to the caller.

units.title: Lazy iteration with generators
units.summary: Yield values on demand and reason about consumed iterators.
lesson: A function containing yield produces a generator iterator when called. It runs lazily: each next() resumes it until the next yield. Its local state is preserved between yields; return ends the generator.

A generator iterator is consumed as you advance it. It does not start over when reused. A generator expression also creates values lazily, while a list comprehension builds a whole list immediately. Laziness can reduce memory for large streams.
units.takeaway: yield suspends execution with state intact; an exhausted iterator does not restart itself.

units.title: Ask your first data question
units.summary: Select columns and filter rows with a clear SQL query.
lesson: SELECT chooses the columns to return and FROM names the source table. WHERE filters individual rows before they reach the result. Text literals use single quotes. Numeric literals such as 18 do not need quotes.

In this unit, learners(id, name, age) contains one row per learner. Use >= for an inclusive lower bound. ORDER BY sorts the result; without it, do not rely on a particular row order. These exercises use SQL compatible with SQLite.
units.example:
SELECT name
FROM learners
WHERE age >= 18
ORDER BY name;
units.takeaway: SELECT picks columns; WHERE picks rows. Use ORDER BY when order matters.

units.title: Summarize rows into groups
units.summary: Aggregate data and filter the resulting groups.
lesson: GROUP BY combines rows with equal grouping values. Aggregate functions such as COUNT(*) and SUM(amount) compute one result per group. In orders(id, customer_id, amount), grouping by customer_id lets us summarize each customer.

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(*) counts rows, including rows whose individual columns contain NULL. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL.
units.example:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
units.takeaway: Use WHERE for input rows and HAVING for aggregate conditions.

exercises.code:

GROUP BY customer_id

units.title: Keep the rows. Add the insight.
units.summary: Use window functions for ranking and running totals.
lesson: Window functions calculate across related rows while keeping each input row. OVER defines the window. PARTITION BY separates independent groups and ORDER BY defines order inside each partition. GROUP BY, in contrast, collapses rows into groups.

For sales(id, team, amount), a running total can use SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY team ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Assume id is unique. ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique position; include a unique tie-breaker in ORDER BY for deterministic numbering.
units.takeaway: A window adds a calculation to each row; partition and ordering define which rows contribute.

units.title: From working file to commit
units.summary: Understand the working tree, staging area and commit history.
lesson: Git tracks snapshots. Your working tree contains editable files; the staging area (index) contains the next proposed snapshot. git add copies the current version of a file into the staging area. Later edits need to be staged again.

git status shows staged and unstaged changes. git commit records the staged snapshot, not every working file. A commit is local; it is not automatically uploaded to a remote. Use small, descriptive commits. These are learning examples, not commands executed by WeCode.
units.example:
git status
git add notes.py
git commit -m "Add learning notes"
units.takeaway: Stage the intended file version before committing; local commits and remote publishing are separate.

units.title: Work safely across branches
units.summary: Create an isolated branch and merge it into the intended target.
lesson: A branch names a line of development. git switch -c feature/notes creates a branch from the current commit and switches to it. New commits advance the branch you have checked out. Check git status before switching, because uncommitted changes can block or complicate a switch.

To bring feature/notes into main, switch to main first, then run git merge feature/notes. If conflicts occur, inspect and edit the conflicted files, stage the resolved versions, and complete the merge. A conflict needs human judgment, not blindly accepting one side.
units.example:
git switch -c feature/notes
# Edit, stage and commit your change
git switch main
git merge feature/notes
units.takeaway: The current branch is the merge destination; the merge argument is the source branch.

options.text: Either branch; the result is identical

units.title: Undo changes without rewriting trust
units.summary: Choose between reverting a shared commit and unstaging a file.
lesson: Undoing is context-dependent. git revert creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit, keeping history intact. For an ordinary non-merge commit already shared with others, revert is usually safer than moving branch history backward with reset. Reverting a merge requires additional parent-selection decisions outside this unit.

git restore --staged notes.py restores the index entry from HEAD by default, leaving working-tree edits in place. git restore notes.py without --staged can discard unstaged file changes; these operations are not interchangeable. Always inspect git status and your diff before undoing.
units.example:
git status
# Unstage notes.py but keep its working-tree edits:
git restore --staged notes.py
# Reverse an ordinary, already-shared commit:
git revert abc1234
units.takeaway: Use a new revert commit for shared history; unstage separately from discarding working edits.
